opus-5.5.text:
Yeah, I think the reward model is really the crux of the whole thing. In PPO you're essentially optimizing the policy against whatever signal the reward model gives you, so the policy can only ever be as good as that signal. If the reward model has blind spots or quirks, the policy will find them. That's the classic reward hacking problem: the policy learns to produce outputs that score highly without actually being better. You see things like responses getting longer and longer, or adopting a confident tone, because the reward model happened to correlate those features with quality.

So I think of the reward model as a proxy, and a fairly fragile one. It's trained on a limited set of human preference comparisons, and once the policy starts drifting away from the distribution those comparisons came from, the reward model is extrapolating, and you really can't trust it there. That's part of why you have the KL penalty against the reference model in PPO. It's partly a regularizer to keep the policy close to where the reward model is still reliable.

That's also why there's been so much interest in alternatives. Methods like DPO fold the reward model into the policy objective directly, so you skip training a separate reward model and the whole PPO loop. And for domains like math or code, people are moving toward verifiable rewards: you check whether the answer is correct or whether the tests pass. That's much harder to hack than a learned preference model. I think that shift has been a big part of the recent progress on reasoning models, because you can optimize much harder against a signal you actually trust.

So my view is that the reward model is necessary when you don't have a ground-truth signal, but you should be skeptical of it. Invest in making it robust, and wherever you can replace it with something verifiable, that's usually the better choice.

r002.rationale: It defines reward hacking as the policy producing outputs that score highly without being better, by exploiting reward-model blind spots or quirks.

fable-5.1.text:
Yeah, so I think the reward model is really the crux of the whole thing, honestly. In PPO, or RLHF more broadly, the policy is only ever going to be as good as the signal it's optimizing against. So the reward model is essentially a learned proxy for human preferences, and the whole game is: how faithful is that proxy, and how far can you push against it before it breaks?

And it does break. That's the thing people underestimate. You train a reward model on, say, a few hundred thousand pairwise comparisons, and it's a pretty good predictor in distribution. But then PPO is an optimizer, it's actively searching for outputs that score highly, and it will find the regions where the reward model is miscalibrated. That's reward hacking. You see things like the policy becoming overly verbose because the reward model has a slight length bias, or adopting certain stylistic tics, lots of hedging, lots of bullet points, whatever happened to correlate with preference in the training data.

So a lot of what you're doing in practice is managing that gap. The KL penalty against the reference policy is one piece of that, it keeps you from wandering too far into territory the reward model has never seen. But I'd argue the more important lever is the reward model itself: the quality and diversity of the preference data, whether you ensemble reward models, whether you keep iterating on it with fresh data from the current policy so it stays in distribution. The iterative setups, where you collect new comparisons after each round of PPO and retrain the reward model, those tend to work a lot better than training it once and treating it as fixed.

The other thing I'd say is that the reward model is where a lot of the interesting scaling questions live. It's usually a smaller model than the policy, partly for cost reasons, and that creates this asymmetry where the student is more capable than the judge. There's been some nice work on how reward model accuracy scales and how that interacts with how much RL you can safely do, and the rough picture is that a stronger reward model buys you more optimization headroom before you start seeing degradation.

And then of course there's the whole movement toward not having a separate reward model at all, things like DPO, where you fold the preference signal directly into the policy objective. I think those are attractive for simplicity, but you lose something too. Having an explicit reward model gives you an artifact you can inspect, evaluate, probe for biases. When it's implicit, that becomes harder. So I don't think the reward model is going away, I think we're going to see it become more sophisticated, more verifiable, maybe grounded in things like execution or formal checks where that's possible, rather than purely learned from preferences.

r002.rationale: It explains that PPO searches for outputs that score highly by finding miscalibrated regions of the reward model, calling this reward hacking.

astra-6.text:
I think of the reward model as a learned proxy for what we actually want. Typically, you train it on preference pairs: given two responses to the same prompt, which one does a human prefer? Then, during PPO, the policy generates a response and the reward model gives it a score. PPO uses that signal to update the policy toward responses that score better.

The tricky part is that a higher reward-model score doesn’t necessarily mean a better response. The policy can discover ways to exploit the reward model’s mistakes. So you usually include a KL penalty to keep the policy from moving too far from a reference model, and you still need separate evaluations to check whether the improvements are real. The reward model gives you a scalable training signal, but it’s an imperfect measure of the behavior you care about.

sol-6.1.text:
I think of the reward model as a learned proxy for what we actually want. You train it on human preferences—say, which of two responses people prefer—and then in PPO it scores the responses generated by the policy. That score provides the signal for improving the policy, usually alongside a KL penalty that keeps it from drifting too far from the reference model.

The challenge is that getting a higher reward doesn’t necessarily mean producing a better answer. The policy can learn to exploit weaknesses in the reward model. So the reward model is really important, but you also need to check whether improvements in its scores translate into improvements that humans actually care about.
